title: Low-level environmental lead exposure in childhood and adult intellectual function: a follow-up study.
ehr_evidence: The data source was a prospective birth cohort established among babies born at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston (1979-1981), with blood-lead concentrations measured from umbilical cord and via capillary/venipuncture samples at ages 6, 12, 18, 24, 57 months and 10 years, plus neuropsychological testing (WASI) and questionnaires collected for the study, not electronic health records.
summary: A follow-up of a prospective cohort of adults aged 28-30 years from the Boston area examined the association between low-level childhood blood-lead concentrations and adult Full-Scale IQ measured by WASI.
key_findings: Average late childhood blood-lead concentration (mean of concentrations at ages 4 and 10 years) had the strongest relationship with Full-Scale IQ (b = -1.89 ± 0.70, p = 0.01, 95% CI -3.30, -0.47).
Full-Scale IQ was significantly related to blood-lead concentration at 6 months (b = -1.66 ± 0.75, p = 0.03), 4 years (b = -0.90 ± 0.41, p = 0.03) and 10 years (b = -1.95 ± 0.80, p = 0.02).
Verbal IQ was significantly related to blood-lead concentration at 10 years (p = 0.001).

Adjusting for maternal IQ altered the significance of the regression coefficient, reducing the estimate from -1.89 (-3.30, -0.47) to -1.11 (-2.29, 0.06), so the confounding effect of maternal IQ could not be excluded.
captured_features: Blood-lead concentrations at cord, 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, 4 years and 10 years
Average and average late childhood blood-lead concentrations
WASI Full-Scale IQ, Verbal IQ and Performance IQ
Maternal IQ, HOME score, birth weight, gestational age, birth order, sex, race, maternal education and tobacco/alcohol use during pregnancy
pathologies_diseases: Reduced adult intellectual function (lower IQ); neurocognitive impairment associated with childhood lead exposure
population: 43 adults aged 28-30 years in the Boston area who participated as newborns/young children in a prospective lead-exposure cohort; predominantly white, college-educated
limitations: Very small sample size (n = 43), which prevented multivariate analysis and evaluation of confounders/interactions.
Potential confounding by maternal IQ could not be excluded.
Limited generalizability due to a homogeneous, highly educated, predominantly white sample.
